title: The Great Consult and the Voyage
setting: Pandemonium and the regions of Hell, then the gates of Hell and the abyss of Chaos
summary: In Pandemonium the devils debate whether to renew the war. Moloch, Belial and Mammon each speak, but Beelzebub carries the vote for Satan’s plan: to strike at God through his new creature, Man. Satan volunteers to go alone, meets his daughter Sin and their son Death at Hell’s gate, and crosses Chaos until he sees the new World hanging from Heaven.

sections.title: Satan opens the council
sections.note: Enthroned in barbaric splendour, Satan argues that Hell at least frees them from envy and faction, and asks for advice: open war or covert guile.

sections.title: Moloch: open war
sections.note: Moloch, the fiercest of the fallen, wants an immediate assault on Heaven. If it destroys them, oblivion is better than this; if not, it is still revenge.

sections.title: Belial: endure and wait
sections.note: Graceful, persuasive Belial argues that war is hopeless and might make things worse; better to keep quiet and hope God’s anger cools. The narrator calls it ‘ignoble ease and peaceful sloth, not peace.’

sections.title: Mammon: an empire in Hell
sections.note: Mammon rejects both war and returning to sing ‘forced hallelujahs.’ He proposes they build their own kingdom from Hell’s gems and gold, ‘free and to none accountable.’

sections.title: Beelzebub proposes the new World
sections.note: The assembly applauds Mammon, but Beelzebub rises like a pillar of state and offers Satan’s scheme: find the new race called Man and seduce it, so God destroys his own work. The devils vote for it with joy.

sections.title: Who will go?
sections.note: Beelzebub describes the perilous journey through the abyss and asks who is equal to it. The whole council sits silent and afraid until Satan rises.

sections.title: Satan volunteers
sections.note: Satan claims the danger as the price of his throne and forbids anyone to join him, shrewdly before rivals can offer. The narrator contrasts the devils’ concord with human quarrels: ‘O shame to men!’

sections.title: The devils’ pastimes and Hell explored
sections.note: While Satan is away the devils race, sing of their fall, argue philosophy, or explore Hell’s four rivers, Lethe and a frozen continent. They find ‘a universe of death.’

sections.title: The gates of Hell
sections.note: Satan flies to the ninefold gates, guarded by two shapes: a woman ending in a serpent, ringed by barking hounds, and a black, shapeless, crowned phantom.

sections.title: Satan and Death confront each other
sections.note: Satan and the phantom trade insults and square up like two storm clouds, until the serpent-woman rushes between them.

sections.title: Sin tells her story
sections.note: The portress reveals that she is Sin, born from Satan’s head in Heaven, and that their incestuous union produced Death, who then raped her and fathered the hounds. It is the poem’s darkest allegory.

sections.title: The bargain and the open gates
sections.note: Satan turns smooth and promises Sin and Death a world to feed on. Sin unlocks the gates, which she can open but never shut, and Chaos appears.

sections.title: Into Chaos
sections.note: Satan looks into the abyss, where the elements war without order, then launches himself into it, falls, flounders and struggles on until he reaches the throne of Chaos and Night.

sections.title: Satan bargains with Chaos
sections.note: Satan promises to return the new World to darkness if Chaos shows him the way. Chaos, resentful of losing territory, points him toward Earth hanging near Heaven.

sections.title: Through to the edge of light
sections.note: Satan fights his way upward; the narrator looks ahead to the bridge Sin and Death will build after the Fall. At last Satan sees Heaven and the small World hanging from it on a golden chain.

famous.why: Satan ‘by merit raised to that bad eminence’ is a glittering, ironic portrait of power as parody of Heaven.
Belial’s ‘those thoughts that wander through eternity’ is a moving plea for consciousness itself, from the poem’s most dishonest speaker.
The devils argue ‘fixed fate, free will, foreknowledge absolute, and found no end, in wandering mazes lost,’ which are the poem’s own deepest questions.
‘Rocks, caves, lakes, fens, bogs, dens, and shades of death’ packs a whole landscape into monosyllables, then names it ‘a universe of death.’
Death is described by what cannot be seen: ‘that shape had none,’ with only ‘the likeness of a kingly crown.’
‘Death grinned horrible a ghastly smile’ is one of the most chilling lines in the poem.

themes: The council is a study in political rhetoric: each speech is eloquent and each serves its speaker’s nature.
Satan’s courage is real but self-serving; even his heroism is a performance for rivals.
Sin and Death are an allegory of how evil breeds from pride and turns on its parent.
Chaos is the raw, warring matter from which God makes worlds, and which Satan would gladly return them to.
art: Satan confronting Death at the gates of Hell, spear and dart levelled, while Sin, a woman to the waist and a coiled serpent below, rushes between them with the great key at her side.
